analysis.one_liner: Forces online payday lenders to obey state interest-rate caps and stops them from draining borrowers' bank accounts without permission.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted payday loans made over the internet, phone, and mail. Online lenders often operate from states — or countries — with no interest-rate limits, then pull repayments straight out of borrowers' bank accounts, racking up fees and repeated charges. The bill would have required every small-dollar loan (about $5,000 or less) to follow the interest-rate caps of the state where the borrower lives, banned companies from selling borrowers' financial information to lenders unless they make the loans themselves, let borrowers stop automatic repayments under existing federal protections, and given the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau new tools to go after offshore lenders that dodge U.S. courts. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who take out small-dollar loans online, by phone, or by mail — typically people living paycheck to paycheck facing an emergency expense. The bill would have limited the interest rates and fees they can be charged to what their own state allows, stopped lenders from pulling money out of their bank accounts without clear written permission, and cut off companies that harvest and resell borrowers' Social Security and bank account numbers. State and tribal enforcers would also have gained a practical way to reach offshore lenders that currently operate beyond U.S. courts.

how_it_helps.text: It makes every online, phone, mail, or bank-issued small-dollar loan (about $5,000 or less) obey the interest-rate and fee caps of the state where the borrower lives, closing the loophole lenders used to charge rates those states banned.

It bans lead generation: companies that collect borrowers' Social Security and bank account numbers and sell them to lenders would have to stop unless they make the loan themselves, cutting off a major source of harassment and data misuse.

It lets borrowers stop payments on small-dollar loan repayments under the same federal protections that already apply to recurring transfers, and blocks lenders from pulling money out through remotely created checks the borrower never authorized in writing.

It gives the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and state and tribal enforcers a way to reach offshore lenders that dodge U.S. courts, including by cutting off their access to the U.S. payment system.
It directs a government study of the lack of access to capital on Indian reservations, aimed at addressing why tribal members turn to high-cost lenders in the first place.

analysis.who_pays: Online and offshore payday lenders, lead-generation websites that sell borrower information, and banks that originate payday loans on behalf of other companies would all lose business models built on charging rates and fees that many states have banned. Payment processors would take on new duties to block payments to lenders that violate state law, though the bill shields them from lawsuits for good-faith compliance. Borrowers in states with strict rate caps could lose access to short-term credit altogether if no lender will serve them legally.

drawbacks.text: By requiring online and bank-originated small-dollar loans to comply with state interest-rate caps, the bill could eliminate access to short-term credit entirely in states with strict caps, leaving some borrowers with an unexpected expense and no legal borrowing option.

The bill applies the consumer's home-state law to transactions involving Indian tribes, overriding tribal lending structures in some cases — the bill itself directs a GAO study of capital scarcity on reservations, an acknowledgment that many tribal communities lack mainstream credit access that these lenders partially fill [S2][S3].

Payment processors and banks would bear new compliance duties to block payments to sanctioned lenders, with some operational cost, though the bill shields them from lawsuits for good-faith compliance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to borrowers was real and large: the bill went after the specific tricks — remotely created checks that drain bank accounts without clear authorization, lead-generation sites that resell Social Security and bank numbers, offshore lenders that dodge state courts — that make high-cost online loans far worse than their storefront cousins [S2][S3]. The strongest drawback is honest: state rate caps, which the bill would enforce nationwide, can leave some borrowers with no short-term credit option at all when an emergency hits before payday, and applying state law to tribal lenders raised questions about tribal authority over lending on tribal lands [S2][S3]. A fair reading is that the bill traded less access to very expensive, high-fee credit for fewer debt traps and fewer drained bank accounts — a trade most payday borrowers experience as protection, though some would experience it as a lost option.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee received the bill the day it was introduced and never scheduled action on it, so it expired with the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013, without ever coming to a vote.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator Merkley on July 24, 2012 with two cosponsors, Senator Udall of New Mexico and Senator Durbin.
The bill's only action after introduction was to be read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online and offshore payday lenders, which kept charging rates banned in borrowers' home states and kept collecting payments through unauthorized bank drafts. Borrowers who use these loans continued paying the fees and overdraft charges the bill was written to prevent.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SAFE Lending Act of 2012 on July 24, 2012.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 24, 2012 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, and no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so no one's actual position was recorded; the Senate Banking Committee, whose agenda controlled the bill's fate, never acted on it.

industries.industry: Online payday and small-dollar lenders, including offshore and tribally affiliated operations
industries.note: The bill would force these lenders to obey the interest-rate caps of every state where their borrowers live, which in states with rate caps means the loan business itself becomes illegal. It also exposes offshore lenders that currently operate beyond the reach of U.S. courts to enforcement, including having their payment processing cut off. These protections exist because these loans routinely trap borrowers in repeat fees.

industries.industry: Payday lead generators and loan brokers
industries.note: The bill bans the business of collecting borrowers' sensitive financial information and selling it to lenders unless the company is making the loan itself. These middlemen profit by reselling borrowers' data and matching them to high-cost loans, at the borrowers' expense.

industries.industry: Banks originating small-dollar loans on behalf of payday lenders
industries.note: National banks have been used to export one state's lending rules to borrowers everywhere. The bill explicitly requires loans conducted by insured depository institutions to follow the borrower's home-state law, ending that workaround.

industries.industry: Payment processors and financial transaction providers
industries.note: They would gain new duties to block payments to lenders sanctioned by the CFPB, but the bill pairs that with immunity from most lawsuits for good-faith compliance, so the cost is compliance work rather than liability.

Tribally affiliated online lenders would come under borrowers' state laws, but the bill also directs a GAO study of the shortage of credit capital on reservations — an acknowledgment of the underlying problem the bill asks tribes to give up revenue from.
